stops.name: Assisi, the stall of San Francesco il Piccolino
stops.campa: In the stall beside the merchant's house, while Pietro di Bernardone trades cloth in France, the lady Pica Bourlémont is delivered of a son. In pregnancy she was given a vision that the boy would be a great spiritual leader, and a pilgrim's word that he must be born among the beasts, like the Lord; so she emptied the ground floor into a manger, hay strewn, an ox and an ass led in, and the child is born into a performance of Bethlehem, the first presepe, staged by his mother. She names him Giovanni, after the Baptist. Assisi keeps the little vault to this day.

stops.name: Assisi, Cathedral of San Rufino, the baptism
stops.campa: The infant is carried up the hill to San Rufino, cathedral of the martyr-bishop of Assisi, and baptized Giovanni at the great Romanesque font, his mother's name for him, given for the Baptist. When Pietro rides home from France he will overrule the font and call the boy Francesco: for her French culture, the troubadour poetry, the exquisite cloth of Provence, and the family Bourlémont. A stranger, some say an angel in pilgrim's dress, asks to hold the child, and presses a mark like a cross into his right shoulder before vanishing. The same font will later christen Clare di Favarone.

stops.name: Assisi, Piazza del Comune, king of the revels
stops.campa: Francesco, now the richest young man of the piazza, spends his father's florins faster than the shop earns them. He is elected master of the revels, carries the baton of the tripudianti, and leads the youth of Assisi through the streets at night singing the songs of the troubadours in French. He dresses in parti-colored silks, sews sackcloth to fine cloth for a joke, feeds every table. Celano says he was the first in follies, and yet courteous beyond all of them, and already unable to refuse a beggar who asked for the love of God.

stops.name: Collestrada, the battle with Perugia
stops.campa: War between Assisi and Perugia. Francesco rides out in armor with the commune's cavalry to the hill of Collestrada above the Tiber crossing, and there in November 1202 the men of Assisi are broken and slaughtered; the chroniclers say the fields were red down to Ponte San Giovanni. Because his armor shows him worth a ransom, Francesco is not butchered with the foot-soldiers but taken alive, roped, and marched to Perugia. He is twenty years old and has seen the face of war.

stops.name: Perugia, the year in the pits
stops.campa: A year in the underground prisons of Perugia. His fellow captives, nobles of Assisi, sink into rage and melancholy; Francesco alone laughs and sings in his chains, until they think him mad. He befriends the one knight so bitter that all the others shun him. When they ask how he can rejoice in a Perugian pit, he gives them the first prophecy of his life, and the canon records it. Fever takes hold of him in the damp; by the time his father ransoms him, late in 1203, he is a sick man.
stops.quote: What do you think will become of me? You will see that one day I shall be adored by the whole world.

stops.name: Assisi, the sickbed and the stale world
stops.campa: Long illness after the ransom. When Francesco can walk again he goes out leaning on a stick to look at the countryside he loved, the vines, Subasio, the plain toward Foligno, and finds to his astonishment that none of it gives him any joy. The beauty of the fields has gone flat, and he wonders at the change in himself, Celano says, and begins to despise what he had admired. The sickness of the body has opened a crack in the merchant's son through which another life is already looking in.

stops.name: Spoleto, the dream of the arms
stops.campa: Restored, Francesco buys splendid armor to ride south to Apulia and win knighthood in the wars under Walter of Brienne. He gets no farther than Spoleto. In the night a voice comes to him in a dream that has already shown him a palace hung with arms: 'Who can do more for you, the lord or the servant?' 'The lord,' he answers. 'Then why do you leave the lord for the servant?' Francesco asks the question that unmakes his knighthood, hears 'Go home; it shall be shown you what to do,' and at dawn turns his horse back toward Assisi.
stops.quote: Lord, what do you want me to do?

stops.name: The plain below Assisi, the kiss of the leper
stops.campa: Riding on the plain near the lazar-house of San Lazzaro d'Arce, Francesco meets the thing he loathes most in the world: a leper, standing in the road. Everything in him recoils; nothing in him obeys. He dismounts, puts money in the ruined hand, and kisses it, and the leper gives him the kiss of peace in return. When he has ridden on and looks back, the canon says, the open plain is empty. In his Testament, dying, he dates his whole life from this road.
stops.quote: When I was in sin, it seemed too bitter to me to see lepers. And the Lord Himself led me among them, and I showed mercy to them. And when I left them, what had seemed bitter to me was turned into sweetness of soul and body.

stops.name: Rome, the beggar's rags at St. Peter's
stops.campa: On pilgrimage to the tomb of the Apostle, Francesco watches the pilgrims drop small coins through the grate and, disgusted at their meanness toward the Prince of the Apostles, flings in his whole purse with a crash that turns every head. Outside in the portico he borrows the rags of a beggar, gives the man his own clothes, and stands all day among the poor of St. Peter's with his hand out, begging in French for the joy of it. He is rehearsing, in borrowed rags, the rest of his life.

stops.name: San Damiano, the crucifix speaks
stops.campa: In the half-ruined chapel of San Damiano below the walls, Francesco kneels before a painted Byzantine crucifix. The lips of the image part and the crucified Christ speaks to him by name, three times: 'Francis, go and repair my house, which as you see is falling wholly into ruin.' He takes the command with a merchant's literalness: stones, mortar, this chapel, not yet knowing the house is the Church itself. Trembling and amazed, Celano says, he rises and sets his whole heart on obeying. The prayer he made before that cross the Order keeps to this day.
stops.quote: Most High, glorious God, enlighten the darkness of my heart, and give me true faith, certain hope and perfect charity, sense and knowledge, Lord, that I may carry out Your holy and true command.
stops.quote_source: The Prayer before the Crucifix (Oratio ante crucifixum), earliest writings of Francis

stops.name: Foligno, the cloth and the horse sold
stops.campa: Obedient to the crucifix and still his father's son, Francesco loads a horse with scarlet cloth from the shop and rides to the market of Foligno, where he sells the cloth, and then, a merchant's flourish, sells the horse out from under himself. He walks the ten miles back and offers the whole purse to the poor priest of San Damiano for oil and stones. The priest, fearing Pietro di Bernardone, refuses the money; Francesco tosses it on a windowsill like dust, and asks instead to stay.

stops.name: Assisi, the renunciation before the bishop
stops.campa: Pietro di Bernardone, whose chains in the cellar his wife undid, Pica loosing her son, hauls him before Bishop Guido in the court by Santa Maria Maggiore to disinherit him and recover the money. Francesco returns the coins, and then everything else: he strips naked before the whole city, lays his clothes at his father's feet, and the bishop wraps his mantle around him. From under the mantle the son declares the exchange of fathers. Afterward his mother consoles him: they share one name, Giovanna and Giovanni, one troubadour fire; he is always her son and a Bourlémont. He goes out from Assisi owning nothing, singing.
stops.quote: Until now I have called Pietro di Bernardone my father. From now on I can say freely: 'Our Father, who art in heaven,' since I have returned to him all his money and all my clothes.
stops.quote_source: Legend of the Three Companions 20; Thomas of Celano, Vita Prima 15
